cells.tense: Right now you're the one tending this, and you know it — deciding what gets fed and what gets left alone, without needing to grip anything.
cells.ask: At the end of one day this week, say out loud what the day asked of you and what it returned — let someone hear the accounting.
cells.core:
You're tending something that's actually growing, and you're doing it deliberately — not by force, not by hovering, but by knowing what it needs and giving that, then stepping back far enough to see how it all fits. That stepping back is the whole trick: you're inside the work and outside it at the same time, which is why your care lands instead of smothering. You can hold two demands at once without picking a favorite, and both of them stay alive because of it.

Because you can see the pattern, you already know when to let a thing finish. Letting it finish — and saying so, out loud, to someone who can hear it — is what your tending has been for. The saying is not a victory lap. It's the last step of the work, and it's what lets your hands come off cleanly.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending what's growing, and you know when to let it be done.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, deliberate care
cells.place: where you stand back far enough to see how the whole thing fits together

cells.tense: You're already living in a version of this that hasn't arrived yet, bracing for demands that haven't been made and arranging everything for a season still out of reach.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've been trying to make happen and let it land on its own this week — then notice what you feel when it does.
cells.core:
You're tending harder than the thing needs — reaching ahead of it, arranging conditions for a future you can't actually write, and calling the tension care. The care is real. The bracing isn't the care. Somewhere under the reaching is a picture of how it should all turn out, and you're spending the present trying to guarantee it. At full strength this looks like a hand steady enough to hold two needs at once; right now the hand is clenched around an outcome instead.

Let one thing come to you instead of hauling it forward. That's not abandoning the work; it's letting the work be finished by time instead of by pressure. What arrives on its own is yours in a way that nothing forced ever is — and it leaves you something to enjoy rather than something to keep defending.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending a future that hasn't asked for you yet.

cells.tense: You stopped tending this some time ago, and you're still standing at the spot where you stopped — the care is there, the hands aren't.
cells.ask: Pick the smallest living thing in your care and do one plain act for it today — water, feed, mend — and let that be enough.
cells.core:
Tending well looks like this: you notice what a thing needs before it asks, you give it that, and you keep your hands on it long enough for the thing to take root. You don't force it and you don't hover. Watching something you kept alive turn out well is its own reward, and the strength of the work is that it keeps going — day after day, long after the first interest has worn off.

That's the part that stopped. You know how to tend things. You can see what needs what, you can feel the pattern, and you're not doing it — not because you stopped caring but because the doing went quiet. The capacity didn't leave. It just doesn't have a hand on anything at the moment.

Start smaller than feels reasonable. One thing, today, kept alive. Not a plan for everything — just the next small act for the one thing in front of you.
cells.sheetLine: The care is still there. It just doesn't have a hand on anything.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, deliberate care
cells.place: where you stand back far enough to see how the whole thing fits together

cells.tense: You're already shaping what grows around you and you're keeping your own name off it — the tending happens, and you talk about it like it happened on its own.
cells.ask: Say plainly, to one person, that you're the one keeping something alive — just the fact of it, without dressing it up.
cells.core:
At its best, this work is invisible: you notice what a thing needs before it asks, you supply it without ceremony, and the thing thrives in a way that looks like nothing happened. No one sees the small repeated acts — the checking, the adjusting, the starting over — and that invisibility is part of what makes it clean. You are good at this partly because you never make it about you.

That's also where it slips. You've been tending something for a while, holding the conditions, and you'd describe it as just how things are, or someone else's doing, or nothing worth mentioning. The tending is real. The claim on it has gone missing.

Say it once, plainly, to someone who can hear it. Not a boast — an acknowledgment, which is different. Naming it is what lets it be finished rather than endlessly carried.
cells.sheetLine: You're already keeping this alive. You just haven't put your name on it.
